Politico is…
articles.body:
The White House on Monday will prohibit Politico from boarding Air Force One and fulfilling its pool duties covering President Trump.

Journalists from the outlet will not be allowed on the plane, CNN first reported , meaning there will be no print representative providing reports on the president’s statements and movements for the day.

Politico is one of three news outlets Trump banned from the White House last month, a move that sparked a lawsuit on First Amendment grounds. In response, a federal judge ruled the administration had violated the news organizations’ due process rights.

Journalists for all three outlets, CNN, Politico and MS NOW, were eventually allowed to reenter the White House, but the administration has since sought to keep CNN from carrying out its TV pool duties on two occasions.

The White House did not return a request for comment.

Trump’s initial ban came in connection with what the president said was the outlet’s publishing of “fake news” that he and his attorneys argue put national security at risk.

Some Trump allies have defended the ban, arguing journalists do not have a right to access “special” spaces around the president, like the Oval Office and Air Force One.

Trump last year banned The Associated Press from certain West Wing spaces over the outlet’s refusal to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” in its widely cited stylebook after Trump changed the name.

After CNN was blocked from its TV pool duties last week, an attorney for the outlet asked a judge to rule on the issue of access as it relates to pool coverage of the president specifically.

A hearing in the case is set for Thursday.

images.caption: Network stands up are seen outside the White House in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 23, 2026. CNN, MS NOW and Politico have their first court appearance with the Trump administration to regain access.

articles.title: House GOP bill moves to close whistleblower gaps exposed by Minnesota Medicaid fraud scandal
articles.summary: A new House GOP bill would shield Medicaid whistleblowers from retaliation after Minnesota workers alleged firings and surveillance for flagging fraud.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Whistleblowers who pulled back the curtain on Medicaid fraud that allegedly cost taxpayers millions of dollars in states like Minnesota could gain new protections under a House GOP bill after alleging they faced retaliation from state leaders. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, unveiled the Medicaid Whistleblower Protection Act, which would establish federal protections nationwide for state and local Medicaid workers who report early warning signs of fraud, including contracting irregularities and unusual financial transactions. "No public servant should have to choose between their conscience and their livelihood," Miller-Meeks said in a press release exclusively obtained by Fox News Digital. "Whistleblowers who report fraud, waste and abuse in Medicaid are protecting taxpayer dollars and the vulnerable people this program is meant to serve, and they deserve real protection, not retaliation." The bill would prevent employers from firing, demoting, threatening, harassing or discriminating against Medicaid workers who report fraud, violations of law, gross mismanagement, abuse of authority or dangers to public health or safety. MINNESOTA 'TRIED TO COVER UP FRAUD ALLEGATIONS,' FORMER STATE TROOPER ALLEGES Workers who face retaliation could also receive reinstatement, twice their back pay plus interest, attorneys' fees and punitive damages. The legislation follows a January letter from more than 30 current and former Minnesota Department of Human Services employees highlighting a "pattern of retaliation" for flagging fraud as early as 2019, with some alleging they faced surveillance, investigations, reassignment and termination. "I will fight to make sure the people willing to tell the truth are protected, not silenced." Miller-Meeks said. Several Republican lawmakers grilled Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison in March over the letter and rampant fraud in the state, questioning when they first learned about the schemes and allegations of retaliation. When pressed on the retaliation claims, Walz said he was "not specifically" aware of them and repeatedly declined to address the allegations. The fraud involved more than $90 million in alleged fraudulent claims tied to multiple state-funded assistance programs. WALZ REMOVES TOP MINNESOTA OFFICIAL ON EVE OF ‘GAUNTLET’ HEARING OVER FRAUD SCANDAL Minnesota state Rep. Kristin Robbins, chair of the House Fraud Prevention and State Agency Oversight Committee, backed the bill, saying politicians and agency leaders target whistleblowers to protect "their political base." "The federal, state and county workers who run these programs are often the first to see red flags, but, as we have seen time and again in Minnesota, if they dare to point it out, they are called racist, accused of creating a hostile work environment, demoted, reassigned or otherwise harmed personally and professionally," Robbins said. The bill is one of 14 measures in House Energy and Commerce Republicans' "Continuing the Fight Against Fraud" package, led by Chairman Brett Guthrie, R-Ky. The package aims to detect fraud more easily, recover improper payments and increase accountability. Another measure in the package led by Miller-Meeks, the WALZ Act, would require the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General to open investigations into any program that sees a 10% or greater increase in total payments over any six-month period within a fiscal year. WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE Guthrie blamed oversight failures under the Biden administration for allowing fraud to "go unchecked in government health programs." "Every dollar stolen by fraudsters or wasted on improper payments is a dollar taken away from supporting families in need who rely on these programs," he said. The legislation would take effect Jan. 1, 2028, amid the Trump administration’s continued crackdown on fraud through an anti-fraud task force led by Vice President JD Vance. articles.title: Trump on protesters at site of proposed arch: ‘Do these people not have jobs?’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday criticized protesters who gathered in Washington last week to oppose his triumphal arch project. “Do these people not have jobs?” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. The president also shared images of the demonstrators — including one photo with Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) — who have pushed back against the…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday criticized protesters who gathered in Washington last week to oppose his triumphal arch project .

“Do these people not have jobs?” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social .

The president also shared images of the demonstrators — including one photo with Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) — who have pushed back against the construction of a $250 million arch in Washington’s Memorial Circle. Many critics have called it a “vanity project” and argued the structure would block views of Arlington National Cemetery.

Protesters in the pictures can be seen holding signs with messages like “veterans over vanity” and “arch of corruption.” One sign also reads “sacred space no snipers,” referring to Trump’s claim that the arch will be a military complex used to dock drones and serve as a perch for snipers.

Duckworth, an outspoken critic of the project, has argued the structure would cause potential problems for the already complicated Washington airspace.

The project has also been opposed by a number of veteran and citizen groups in the Washington area. At least one House Republican, Rep. Mike Simpson (Idaho), has also criticized the construction over the potential use of Pentagon funding.

“If it was my choice, I wouldn’t put any of that money into the arch,” Simpson told reporters last month, suggesting the military is already short on funding.

The U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, which is made up of seven Trump-appointed panelists, approved the structure’s design earlier this year. A group of Vietnam War veterans later sued to stop its construction.

The arch is one of many renovation projects the president has dedicated his time to in the nation’s capital since returning to the Oval Office.

Other endeavors include the White House ballroom , including the demolition of the East Wing , Rose Garden and helipad upgrades , changes to the Kennedy Center and the installation of statues on the district’s Freedom Plaza.

The federal government has monitored elections since the 1960s and the DOJ will assure federal law is being enforced properly, Blanche told Shannon Bream on “Fox News Sunday.” “They’re not going…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) plan to send 1,000 election monitors to polling places on Election Day.

The federal government has monitored elections since the 1960s and the DOJ will assure federal law is being enforced properly, Blanche told Shannon Bream on “Fox News Sunday.”

“They’re not going to Republican states, they’re not going to Democrat states, they are going to every state to make sure our elections are carried out legally, fairly and appropriately,” he added.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The attorney general criticized Democratic lawmakers for “fearmongering” in claiming the DOJ is trying to intimidate voters.

“This administration, President Trump, is doing the same thing that every single administration has done in our generation, in multiple generations,” Blanche said. “We’re making sure that federal law is being enforced appropriately.”

Trump has made election integrity a key part of his agenda, repeatedly doubting the security and validity of American elections. He has pushed Congress to pass his voter identification and restrictive mail-in voting legislation, the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act.

The federal government has long deployed DOJ officials to polling sites to assure compliance with civil rights and voting laws. Blanche said the DOJ is hoping to have “a thousand or more” monitors stationed during November’s midterms.

The attorney general said the claim that “armed federal agents” will be deployed to the polls is “completely false.”

articles.title: Kelly: Hegseth’s firings of top generals, admirals damage ‘our readiness’
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ouster of top generals and admirals from the U.S. military are “damaging our readiness,” according to Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), a retired astronaut and Navy captain. A member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Kelly said Hegseth’s intended 20 percent reduction of the top of the ranks — announced last week…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ouster of top generals and admirals from the U.S. military are “damaging our readiness,” according to Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), a retired astronaut and Navy captain.

A member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Kelly said Hegseth’s intended 20 percent reduction of the top of the ranks — announced last week — would only hurt national security.

“When you hurt readiness, it means that all of us … are less safe because we have the most unqualified secretary of Defense we’ve ever had in this country’s history,” Kelly said Sunday on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

He also accused Hegseth of often firing people “because of the color of their skin or because they’re women.”

The Defense secretary last week defended the reduction in senior officers’ ranks as promoting “accountability” and “long overdue,” in a speech at the Marine Corps Base in Quantico, Va.

Several top Republican senators have since said they were blindsided by the decision and are not pleased about the lack of consultation with Congress.

These GOP lawmakers also worry too many experienced and highly qualified generals and admirals are being pushed out because of political or ideological reasons.

Adding to the furor is Hegseth’s reported intervention to stop the promotion of several Army officers, including Black and female officers who had been on track to become one-star generals.

Hegseth also blocked the promotion of nine Navy officers who had been selected by a board of senior admirals, The New York Times reported in June.

Prior to that, Hegseth in February 2025 fired Adm. Lisa Franchetti, the first woman to serve as chief of Naval Operations — a move that was criticized by Democratic lawmakers.

The Pentagon has denied claims that promotions and forced retirements were based on identity politics, with Hegseth telling the audience during his address at Quantico that his agency remains “colorblind, gender-neutral and merit-based.”

The Defense secretary and Kelly have often sparred publicly since Hegseth, an Army veteran and former Fox News host, was appointed to lead the Pentagon.

Hegseth’s campaign to punish Kelly for appearing in a video, in which six Democrats told members of the military to refuse illegal orders, has been a loser in court so far.

articles.title: Paxton raises $18M in third quarter
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) raised $18 million in the third quarter as he trails Democrat James Talarico in polls on the contentious Texas Senate race. Paxton’s July-to-September haul is double the $9 million he raised in the second quarter of the year, adding to what’s already the most expensive Senate race of the…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) raised $18 million in the third quarter as he trails Democrat James Talarico in polls on the contentious Texas Senate race.

Paxton’s July-to-September haul is double the $9 million he raised in the second quarter of the year, adding to what’s already the most expensive Senate race of the cycle.

Talarico has not yet released his third-quarter numbers but raised more than $30 million in the second quarter.

“Republicans from all corners of Texas have given to the campaign because they know what’s at stake,” said Nick Maddux, senior adviser to the Paxton campaign, in a release.

Funds are flooding into the Texas Senate race as Democrats grow bullish about their first statewide flip in decades — and as Republicans fret about Paxton’s lag in the polls.

President Trump’s MAGA Inc. dropped $10 million into the race in early September, and Republicans put the spotlight on Paxton, who defeated incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) for the party nod, when they hosted their midterm convention in Dallas last month.

But Paxton has struggled for momentum in the red stronghold. His controversial record as the Lone Star State’s top prosecutor has raised concerns about his general election viability — and, in audio shared by the New York Times, Paxton contended that the midterm convention “dropped our numbers.”

Trump, who recently called him a “pain in the a‑‑,” is expected to rally with Paxton in San Antonio later this week.

Cook Political Report shifted the race away from Republicans to a “toss up” rating in August. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) also considers it a coin flip, but narrowly favors Democrats, giving Talarico a 56 percent probability of flipping the seat.

DDHQ’s latest polling averages show Talarico nearly 3 points ahead of Paxton, after a smaller gap between the Senate rivals this summer.

articles.title: Vanity Fair’s ‘new establishment’ list names Vance as Trump ‘heir’ and Rubio as ‘spare’
articles.summary: Vanity Fair on Monday released its “New Establishment 2026” list and included several Trump administration officials, referring to Vice President Vance as the “MAGA heir” but naming Secretary of State Marco Rubio as the “MAGA spare.” The magazine wrote Vance “had reason for optimism” following President Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025,…
articles.body:
Vanity Fair on Monday released its “New Establishment 2026” list and included several Trump administration officials , referring to Vice President Vance as the “MAGA heir” but naming Secretary of State Marco Rubio as the “MAGA spare.”

The magazine wrote Vance “ had reason for optimism ” following President Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, describing MAGA as “something close to trendy” with Vance as “its de facto prince.”

“‘Communion,’ Vance’s recent book about his conversion to Catholicism, allowed for a splashy media tour that brought him in front of hostile audiences like those of ‘The View,'” Vanity Fair wrote.

“Vance took some heat for embarking on that tour while in office (shouldn’t the vice president have better things to do during a war in the Middle East?), but his talk show appearances seem to have appealed to the viewer in chief: Trump, who, according to several reports, currently considers Vance his heir apparent,” the outlet added.

Vanity Fair said readers know the memes of Rubio “ stone-faced on a sofa in the Oval Office, newly appointed to a role just vacated by an embarrassed or embattled official of some sort” before naming some examples of these AI-generated memes.

“Rubio’s role has afforded him vast powers over an administration that’s shaping the world at its whims,” the magazine wrote , including various acts overseen by the former Florida senator — from the U.S. blockade on Cuba to the raid that led to Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro’s capture.

“All the while, Rubio has telegraphed that he’s having fun with it,” Vanity Fair wrote. “… Trump might be at his most unpopular moment in history, presiding over a war he can’t explain and prices he can’t bring down. Somehow, his man at state seems to be evading the worst of the blame while maintaining a sunny disposition that keeps his name in the 2028 conversation.”

The magazine described both men as having their own Achilles’ heels.

Vance’s included remarks he made about those charged and convicted in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and how the rioters “obviously” should not be pardoned before the president did just that following his inauguration. The outlet also pointed to Trump’s anti-war stance — one that aligned with Vance’s view — prior to launching the Iran war.

As for Rubio, he “may have cultivated an aura of upbeat competence, but it’s hard to see how he’ll emerge from Trump 2.0 unscathed,” Vanity Fair wrote in a short paragraph.

The magazine mentioned the speculation of Vance running to succeed Trump in 2028 but stated that the vice president “remains one of the least popular figures in the entire Trump administration” and warned that convincing Americans to “like him looks, so far, like scaling a mountain.”

Vanity Fair pointed to Rubio’s growing foreign policy portfolio but noted that his boss is “hopelessly fixated on stomping around the globe, a tendency that’s created a sweeping portfolio of problems for Rubio to solve.” It referred to how Vance, not Rubio, was initially sent to negotiate a peace deal with Iran, though these talks produced no immediate results.

The authors did not delve into speculation about Rubio as a potential Republican presidential contender in 2028. Both he and Vance have been seen as possible torchbearers to carry on Trump’s legacy, but neither of them has publicly stated that they intend to run.

The “new establishment” list is comprised of 50 people or groups “who have defined the moment” — specifically referring to figures in 2026 who “should inspire complicated feelings.” Vance and Rubio were joined by two of the president’s children, Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump, as well as the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

The list starts with tech leaders in artificial intelligence, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. Vanity Fair also named New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan Piker and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), along with other democratic socialist candidates and lawmakers among the notable names of the year.

Other names included were California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D); Pope Leo XIV; CNN’s Kaitlan Collins; directors Christopher Nolan and Ryan Coogler; television writers Taylor Sheridan and Ryan Murphy; and Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk.

articles.title: Donald Trump says a 'threat' led US to move bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.summary: The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed the B1 bombers from the base in England back to their home stations in America.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.

The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.

Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.

Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford?

What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites?

Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.

Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.

"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."

He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who.

The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.

One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.

"Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.

Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.

RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.

Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.

Following the release of the first five men , Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.

Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.

Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.

He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."

Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.

Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency.

However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added.

The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

articles.title: Replica Oval Office near the White House gets a new Trump makeover. Gold is everywhere
articles.summary: The People’s House museum exhibit has overhauled its replica Oval Office for visitors to experience President Donald Trump’s second-term design choices.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — It’s glitzier. And there’s way more gold.

The People’s House museum exhibit has overhauled its replica Oval Office for visitors to experience President Donald Trump’s second-term design choices.

Gleaming vases, golden-hued swirling onlays, two dozen portraits in heavy gilded frames and knickknacks crowding nearly every available surface: the same rococo flourishes that Trump has installed in the world’s most famous workspace have been recreated down to each wall appliqué in a museum just up Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House.

“As political as the Oval Office is, it really is also the office of the American people,” said Luke Boorady, managing director of The People’s House: A White House Experience. “And we want visitors who come here to feel more connected to this space.”

Public tours of the White House do not include the West Wing. So the White House Historical Association set about recreating the Oval Office, opening the exhibit in September 2024. It is the same size as the real one, and visitors often marvel at how small it feels.

A team of specialized designers has been making over the exhibit, visiting Trump’s Oval Office while the Republican president was away. Experts in North Carolina worked to recreate Trump’s many wall appliqués, while one from Indianapolis handled 3D scanning and printing of other specialized objects. California frame-makers did carving by hand for the gold frames of Trump’s chosen 24 portraits, and teams from Canada and Virginia worked on replicas of vases and other tabletop pieces, Boorady said.

There are also two mirrors and a copy of the Declaration of Independence, just like in Trump’s actual office.

The president has molded the White House in his own image

A real estate developer before he became a politician, Trump has revamped the White House to his extravagant tastes as part of his push to leave his mark on the nation’s capital while he is still in office.

When asked by Time magazine last week what he would miss most about the White House after he leaves, Trump said, “This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office.” He said he had asked his chief of staff to make his altered office “a federal landmark.”

In addition to filling the Oval Office with bling, Trump paved over the lawn near the Rose Garden to build a patio space reminiscent of the one at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. He installed a row of presidential portraits along the colonnade between the White House residence and the West Wing.

He erected towering flagpoles on the North and South lawns, renovated the Palm Room and the bathroom that is part of the famous Lincoln Bedroom and ordered restoration work of the North Portico’s front columns .

But Trump seems proudest of the $400 million ballroom that he is building after ordering that the East Wing be demolished . “It relaxes me, actually,” the president said about the ballroom project during an unrelated event last week.

Trump’s sense of ownership of the White House is now such that while recently defending his attempt to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from its grounds , the president had a momentary slip of the tongue. “I don’t have to let them into my — into the people’s house,” he said.

A replica of Trump’s first term Oval Office gets a makeover

When the White House Historical Association first opened its Oval Office duplicate, it mirrored Democratic President Joe Biden’s design. After the 2024 election, the association updated the exhibit to match Trump’s first-term style.

Last week, a crew of 25 people worked from early Monday through late Friday to get the second-term transformation ready, making the finishing touches on Saturday.

Boorady said Biden was the first president to hang double layers of portraits over the Oval Office fireplace. Trump has expanded that all around the room, stacking the walls with portraits including those of George Washington, Andrew Jackson and Benjamin Franklin.

In the real Oval Office, the colors are made more brilliant by using gilded gold leaf. In the replica, crews used a paint solution. Boorady said they did not use gold leaf to protect against chipping or other wear-and-tear from visitors moving through the area.

Trump was once spotted using superglue to try to affix gold ornaments to the Oval Office fireplace, according to Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan in their book “Regime Change.”

But no superglue was needed in the replica office. Crews used laser levels and temporary adhesive to fix items to the walls, checking their work for accuracy against renderings of the actual office before nailing many adornments to the walls.

There are many things in Trump’s Oval Office that have stood the test of time: a beige-patterned rug from the Ronald Reagan era, gold draperies from Bill Clinton’s tenure, and couches and chairs from the George W. Bush White House.

Of course there is a copy of the Resolute Desk . Visitors to the People’s House are allowed to sit in the chairs and behind the replicated desk, which Trump and most presidents have used since it was gifted to President Rutherford B. Hayes in 1880.

The White House Historical Association declined to say how much remaking the replica Oval Office cost. The organization, created in 1961 by first lady Jacqueline Kennedy, receives no government funding, and raises money through private donations and sales of retail merchandise.

Trump briefly stopped by its gift shop during an unannounced visit to the People’s House in August 2025. Asked whether Trump would come for a personal peek at his newly replicated workspace, Boorady replied, “I don’t know” before adding that he is “always welcome.”

images.caption: A replica of President Donald Trump’s Oval Office is updated to the current decor by workers at “The People’s House: A White House Experience,” in Washington, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)

articles.title: Woman sues Trump administration after being shot five times by immigration agent
articles.summary: Marimar Martinez, a Chicago woman who was shot five times by an immigration agent, sued the federal government Monday for damages, with her attorneys saying new analysis of the scene will prove the officer shot her as she was turning her car away from him. Martinez was initially charged in the wake of her shooting…
articles.body:
Marimar Martinez, a Chicago woman who was shot five times by an immigration agent, sued the federal government Monday for damages, with her attorneys saying new analysis of the scene will prove the officer shot her as she was turning her car away from him.

Martinez was initially charged in the wake of her shooting by Border Patrol agent Charles Exum. The suit alleges false arrest and imprisonment, malicious prosecution, emotional distress, and negligence.

Martinez’s attorneys took the unusual step of hring a crime scene analyst in advance of bringing the case.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“We know in this day and age, with 40 [to] 50 percent of America believing everything that comes out of the mouth of a DOJ [Department of Justice] or the current administration’s representative, that we need to show objective proof from Jump Street. We need to show them that their lies are done today, that they can’t twist the truth or keep spinning it because that ends,” said Michael Gallagher, one of the attorneys bringing the case, in a Chicago press conference.

“So with this investigation and this kind of analysis, we think we’ve done that.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not comment on the case or its claims.

“Consistent with policy, Agent Exum was placed on administrative leave,” a spokesperson said.

Shortly after the shooting, the Department of Homeland Security called Martinez a domestic terrorist and said she had tried to attack Exum with her car.

Martinez’s legal team walked through the analysis, noting that shots entered through the passenger side of her front windshield and then later through the side of her car, details they say defy Exum’s explanation that he fired as her vehicle was heading towards him.

“It’s actual, concrete physical evidence and science by an independent expert that shows the agent lied about where he was, and Marimar has been telling the truth,” said Chris Parente, another of Martinez’s attorneys.

The suit, brought under the Federal Tortious Claims Act, does not ask for specific damages and Gallagher said they are most interested in bringing the case to trial before a judge.

“We don’t expect them to ever offer any type of money, which is fine by us. We prefer the verdict,” he said.

Martinez said once the charges against her were dropped, she was prepared to let the matter go until there were two more fatalities at the hands of federal agents in Minneapolis.

“Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims. So I won’t stop. I have a voice, and I do matter, and I don’t want it to keep happening. I don’t. I just don’t. So I want to spread awareness because what’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening,” Martinez said.

articles.title: Permanent daylight saving time: Why this Republican senator disagrees with it, despite Trump’s support
articles.summary: Trump went so far as to share his personal cellphone number online. Still, Sen. Cotton isn’t supporting permanent daylight saving time.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – “It’s said that those who don’t learn from history are doomed to repeat it.”

That’s a line you’ve likely heard in reference to any number of events, from the mundane to the tales recounted in your history books. In this case, Senator Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) would point to an Oct. 2025 floor speech in response to an effort to fast-track the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent in the U.S.

Cotton noted his own opposition to changing the clocks twice a year, contending that “there’s not much to be done” regarding it “unless we’re willing to adopt permanent standard time.”

“Not every human problem has a legislative solution,” he added.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Despite his remarks ( and history ), a version of the Sunshine Protection Act found its way to the Senate again this year. The House passed the bill in July on a 308-117 vote, and President Trump said it would be “a very nice WIN for the Republican Party. Take it!”

The bill, however, faces a dim future in the Senate. Several Republican lawmakers have expressed opposition to it , including Cotton. The chamber has also adjourned until after the midterm election and the end of daylight saving time , which means our clocks will most likely “fall back” as usual in a few weeks.

If you’re bummed by that, you aren’t alone. Trump recently lashed out at Cotton for “holding up a very important Bill,” the Sunshine Protection Act. He shared Cotton’s cellphone number, urging Arkansas residents to call their senator and tell him “it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN.”

In a post to X , Cotton reiterated his stance that “no one likes changing the clock, me included” and again referred to previous efforts by the U.S. to observe permanent daylight saving time. As he did in his floor speech last year, Cotton pointed to a specific group of Americans who could be most impacted by permanent daylight saving time.

Nexstar contacted Cotton’s office for comment and was directed to his X post.

What would change under permanent daylight saving time?

The winter sun would set an hour later than it currently does, and, in turn, rise an hour later than we’re used to, sometimes well after 8 a.m.

In Fayetteville, Arkansas, for example, there would be nearly 90 days between November and March in which the sun would not rise until after 8 a.m. Further north, in, say, Grand Rapids, Michigan, there would be more than 140 sunrises after 8 a.m., and another 55 after 9 a.m.

The interactive table below shows how many winter days would see sunrises after 8 a.m. (or 9 a.m., in some cases), under permanent daylight saving time.

Why permanent daylight saving time has failed before

While it has its supporters , permanent daylight saving time has never stuck around for long in the U.S.

As Cotton noted, part of the reason it was quickly repealed in the early 1970s was because of a decline in public support. Reporting from the time suggests parents may have been among the loudest opponents.

They found themselves sending their children off to school in morning darkness, some armed with flashlights, prompting safety concerns. There were multiple incidents nationwide of children being struck by vehicles while on their way to school, including eight fatalities in Florida .

The U.S. Department of Transportation would find no clear evidence regarding traffic accidents in relation to permanent daylight saving time, but the nation returned to seasonal time change roughly a year after locking the clocks.

Permanent daylight saving time may be bad for our health

In addition to the safety risks, Cotton has previously said that locking the clocks on year-round daylight saving time may not be good for our health.

Health experts largely agree that permanent daylight saving time would disrupt our sleep and circadian rhythm, which could have even greater impacts throughout our lives . Studies have found links to poor student performance , for example, as well as mental health issues, delinquent behaviors, and even employment salaries.

The Senate could still pass the Sunshine Protection Act when they return in mid-November, though Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) had previously cast doubt on its ability to reach the required 60-vote threshold needed to pass. Plus, the current Congress is only expected to remain in session through about mid- to late December.

Congress is also considering two bills in the House that would give states the option to observe year-round daylight saving time, a bill to make half-daylight saving time permanent and a newly introduced bill to make standard time permanent , with exceptions.

For now, though, our clocks appear likely to “fall back” to standard time in the early morning hours of Nov. 1.

articles.title: Trump calls for media outlets to be ‘arrested’ over rally coverage
articles.summary: President Trump said Monday that reporters from The New York Times and other media outlets should be “arrested” over their coverage of his Saturday rally in Ohio. “The Ohio Arena was already full to the brim — And yet these people were still trying to get in,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, sharing a video…
articles.body:
President Trump said Monday that reporters from The New York Times and other media outlets should be “arrested” over their coverage of his Saturday rally in Ohio.

“The Ohio Arena was already full to the brim — And yet these people were still trying to get in,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , sharing a video of people in line for the rally .

New York Times correspondent Katie Rogers wrote Sunday that “several areas of an upper deck were empty” by the time the president finished speaking at Butler High School in Vandalia.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The school’s student center, where the event took place, has a capacity of 4,500 people, Rogers noted.

But Trump denied those details, saying there were no empty seats and “thousands of people had to be turned away” from attending the rally.

“The New York Times, and many other Artificial Media Outlets, should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” the president added, accusing outlets of inflating crowds for Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and downplaying how many people attend his rallies.

“The Arena was totally MAXED OUT, including all upper sections,” Trump wrote in a subsequent post. “What does happen at all of my SOLD OUT Rallies, is that the people in the upper sections tend to migrate down to the Main Floor — The ‘migration’ process always happens!”

The president also shared a video of himself taking the stage at the rally as attendees chanted “USA” multiple times.

“There are thousands of people outside [who] can’t get in. If you’d like to give up your seat, please, we can work it out, get out of here,” Trump said at the rally.

During the rally, the president stumped for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who faces a tough reelection battle against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio). Former NFL coach Jon Gruden also delivered remarks, saying Husted was a friend of his who “will never quit.”

Trump has long targeted the Times and its reporters, accusing the outlet of covering him unfavorably dating to his first presidential campaign.

The Justice Department over the summer subpoenaed the phone records of multiple Times journalists and their family members after they reported on security concerns Secret Service officials had about the Qatari-gifted jet for Air Force One. The department dropped the request days later .

The North Carolina Senate race is viewed as Democrats’ best pickup opportunity, and the party is looking to expand its map into Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

articles.title: Trump says Russia plague reports concerning: Microbes ‘stronger and smarter’
articles.summary: President Trump said Monday he is concerned about the suspected plague case in Russia, saying the U.S. is “looking at it very strongly.” The State Department said Monday it was monitoring the suspected case of pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia. “I hate to see them having it,” Trump told reporters before departing the White…
articles.body:
President Trump said Monday he is concerned about the suspected plague case in Russia, saying the U.S. is “looking at it very strongly.”

The State Department said Monday it was monitoring the suspected case of pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia.

“I hate to see them having it,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House for Nebraska. “It’s a rough disease. We used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter.”

“The germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well anymore,” he said.

Pneumonic plague “is a rare and often fatal disease that can be transmitted by respiratory droplets from animals or persons infected with Yersinia pestis bacteria,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It is different from pneumonia, which is the term for inflammation of the lungs.

NBC News reported Monday that some 200 people were under medical observation in Siberia after a 28-year-old lab worker, who was possibly exposed to the pneumonic plague, died.

On Sunday, the Russian consumer welfare service said the 28-year-old, who worked at an institute combating the plague in Irkutsk, died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” the outlet reported.

Trump said Monday “we’ll help” Russia with the potential outbreak.

A State Department official said Russia has not provided many details on the issue.

“Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” the official said. “Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early. Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world.”

articles.title: Vance-Cruz battle suggests GOP gloves coming off in presidential fight
articles.summary: When Vice President Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) traded increasingly personal barbs over the last few days, one thing was clear: Not only is the 2028 Republican primary officially underway, but the gloves are already coming off. The tiff began when Vance swiped at Cruz last week, saying it was “really obvious” that the…
articles.body:
When Vice President Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) traded increasingly personal barbs over the last few days, one thing was clear: Not only is the 2028 Republican primary officially underway, but the gloves are already coming off.

The tiff began when Vance swiped at Cruz last week, saying it was “really obvious” that the Texas senator was running for president.

Then in an interview over the weekend, Cruz pushed back, saying, “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes,” Cruz told Politico in the interview.

The exchange offered an early glimpse into how top Republicans — who have played nice so far — may switch gears after the midterms.

It also might underscore the nerves surrounding the midterms; Republicans are bracing for bruising losses in the House and Senate, even as they battle to hold their congressional majorities.

Behind the scenes, Republicans are worried about how big midterm losses could translate to the race in 2028. The GOP is faltering in the midterms in large part because of President Trump’s own falling approval ratings. How might that impact Vance in the run-up to 2028?

If the GOP does have a poor midterm election year, does that give momentum to Cruz and other potential Republican presidential candidates who are not a part of the Trump administration?

Trump, for his part, hasn’t picked a successor, seemingly enjoying the competition surrounding Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“Vance should be insecure because of Donald Trump’s poll numbers and the fact that at this point Trump isn’t even willing to commit to his vice president is very telling,” said Republican strategist Susan Del Percio, who does not support the president.

Del Percio explained that Vance finds himself in a precarious spot because he has to appear like there is no distance between himself and the president. And if he starts to look like he’s breaking with Trump, “that could be the beginning of the end” with the president, she said.

“There is no winning for JD Vance,” Del Percio explained. “He’s either too Trump or not enough Trump. And Cruz has found his moment to play on a no-win situation for JD Vance.”

“If you’re Cruz it’s just good politics,” she added. “He’s found a weak spot, and he’s not letting go.”

But one Trump administration official said Monday that if the vice president decides to run, Cruz may realize that it could be an uphill battle for him, which is why he’s taking the early shots at Vance.

The early jockeying comes as Trump’s approval ratings have reached all-time lows — much of which can be attributed to the war in Iran, high gas prices and inflation.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted late last month, for example, showed the president with a 32 percent approval rating, with 66 percent disapproving of his job performance.

A recent Associated Press/NORC poll was even more dire for the commander in chief. That survey showed just 26 percent approved of Trump’s handling of the economy and only 17 percent approved of his handling of the cost of living.

The poll also revealed that 65 percent believed Trump’s policies were more responsible for high costs than factors outside his control while 7 in 10 said his handling of the cost of living was worse than they expected.

But some polling suggests Vance — who opposed the Iran war at the start — has a more favorable rating than Trump.

Last month, a Marquette Law School poll of registered voters in Wisconsin found that 43 percent viewed the vice president favorably, compared to 38 percent who viewed Trump favorably.

Republicans acknowledge that Vance faces a tough road ahead if he is vying for a White House run on the heels of a tumultuous couple of years.

“He is in an unenviable position, especially if we lose the way many are expecting in November,” said one Republican strategist who asked for anonymity to speak candidly. “It’s going to be tough for him to distance himself from anything the administration has done. And the second he begins attacking Trump, he has lost his endorsement and he knows it.”

“And everyone knows Trump’s endorsement still carries a lot of weight,” the strategist added.

A former Trump campaign aide agreed, saying as of now Vance has the support of the president’s network behind him.

“He has the support of Trumpworld, and likely access to Trump’s resources,” the former aide said. “Right now, no one else can say that.”

But the former aide and the GOP strategist acknowledged the administration’s policies do open the doors for other potential candidates, like Cruz, who can distance themselves appropriately.

“I think that’s why you’re starting to see the attacks coming in hot,” the strategist said. “And if we lose, it’s going to get ugly pretty quickly, and I think some other folks might be revving up to enter if that happens.”

Rubio is frequently mentioned as a leading contender for 2028 but has sought to avoid some of the turmoil enveloping the Trump administration. While other Republicans — including many Cabinet secretaries — gathered last month at a GOP convention in Dallas, for example, Rubio traveled on a diplomatic trip to Colombia.

During those travels, he was asked by a reporter if he was one of the most formidable candidates on the Republican side for 2028

“Well, I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time,” Rubio said, according to The Wall Street Journal. “I’m 100 percent focused on my jobs.”

One strategist who is hoping for a Rubio candidacy told The Hill that the secretary of State has been telling donors that he’s not running.

Del Percio predicted that the fights will only get bigger if Republicans lose control of the Senate — especially in Cruz’s home state of Texas, where the state’s Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) is facing off against Democratic Texas state Rep. James Talarico for a Senate seat.

“If Paxton loses, Cruz will go after Vance even more,” she said.

“If nothing else, you ding Vance up a little,” she added. “Because it seems like Vance has gotten one of the main characteristics of his boss down pat, and that is a thin skin.”

articles.title: Supreme Court hears major climate case
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Justices appear unconvinced by oil arguments Several Supreme Court Justices appeared skeptical Monday of a request from oil companies to preemptively block a climate change lawsuit that could hold them liable for climate damages. © Greg Nash Many of the justices raised questions about…
articles.body:
Justices appear unconvinced by oil arguments

Several Supreme Court Justices appeared skeptical Monday of a request from oil companies to preemptively block a climate change lawsuit that could hold them liable for climate damages.

Many of the justices raised questions about the court’s ability to even take up the case at this time.

“A number of the discussions that you’ve had with my colleagues make me think that we’re really early in this case – that this is sort of premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction,” liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Suncor Energy lawyer Kannon Shanmugam.

While Jackson’s skepticism is not necessarily a surprise, several of her conservative colleagues, namely Justices John Roberts and Neil Gorsuch, also asked tough questions of the fossil fuel firm and the Trump administration which backed it.

Suncor, alongside ExxonMobil, has asked the high court to toss a ruling from the Colorado Supreme Court that allowed a suit to proceed. The suit alleged that the energy companies misled the public about their products’ relationship to climate change and created a public nuisance.

The case could have implications for similar litigation around the nation, as states and localities have sued oil and other fossil fuel companies seeking compensation for damages they’ve suffered because of climate change.

The court could rule one of three ways: The justices could expressly block the case or expressly allow it to proceed, or they could rule that they don’t have jurisdiction at this point, which could allow the case to move forward, but could see the issue back at the high court at a later date.

Either of the latter two outcomes could be at least a partial win for the localities, as they would be able to move ahead with their case — at least in the short term.

articles.title: Trump’s deportation agenda haunts him in 2 high-profile House races
articles.summary: President Trump’s deportation agenda is haunting him in two key House races as polls show Latino voters turning on the president and Republicans a month out from the midterm elections. The issue is acutely playing out in Florida’s 27th and Texas’s 15th congressional districts, where incumbent Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) and Monica De La…
articles.body:
President Trump’s deportation agenda is haunting him in two key House races as polls show Latino voters turning on the president and Republicans a month out from the midterm elections.

The issue is acutely playing out in Florida’s 27th and Texas’s 15th congressional districts, where incumbent Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) and Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas), respectively, are facing competitive reelection bids.

Salazar made headlines last month when she released a video filmed in front of the White House, warning Trump that Hispanic voters who supported him in 2024 feel betrayed by his immigration policies.

De La Cruz released her own ad the same day, touting her efforts to release a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

“What they’re doing is they’re trying to show distance between themselves and the president. They’re trying to unanchor themselves because he is so unpopular,” said Mike Madrid, a Republican strategist and Trump critic who specializes in Latino voting behavior and trends.

“The best symbolic way to do that is on the immigration issue,” he continued. “You can’t really distance yourself from him on the economy because nobody knows what his economic policy is day to day. So what are you standing against? The immigration issue is very clear.”

Trump and Salazar carried Florida’s 27th Congressional District by 15 points and 20 points, respectively, in 2024, while he and De La Cruz carried Texas’s 15th Congressional District by 15 points and 14.2 points, respectively.

“They both should be Republican districts on paper,” Madrid said.

Democrats are making a concerted effort to flip the two seats with the party’s campaign arm adding Salazar’s opponent, Eliott Rodriguez, to its “Red to Blue” program. The campaign arm also rolled out a $13 million ad buy in 35 races, including in De La Cruz’s district, on Monday.

In a statement to The Hill, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Bridget Gonzalez accused De La Cruz and Salazar of “trying to rewrite their immigration record.”

“They’ve cheered on Trump’s extremist agenda and out-of-control ICE operations at every turn, and voters can see right through them,” Gonzalez said.

One Republican operative speaking on the condition of anonymity pushed back on the Democratic narrative on the races, arguing Salazar’s and De La Cruz’s stances on immigration are no surprise.

“The Maria Salazar ad, I think, was mostly a surprise to people who have never heard of Maria Salazar,“ the GOP operative said. “It was definitely not a shock to us.”

“Monica De La Cruz, the same thing,” they added.

The lawmakers’ supporters note Salazar introduced the Dignity Act, which calls for a legal “Dignity Status” for immigrants who have resided in the U.S. for years without a criminal history.

De La Cruz has touted her role in helping to secure the release of a family that included two teenage mariachi students in March.

Republicans across the board appear to be in trouble with the Latino voting bloc, which helped to boost Trump and the GOP two years ago.

An NBC News/Telemundo poll released over the weekend showed Democrats leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot 59 percent to 35 percent among Latino voters. Meanwhile, a recent CBS News poll showed 60 percent of Hispanic voters saying they plan to vote Democratic in November, while 39 percent said they planned to vote Republican.

Other polls show Hispanic and Latino voters unhappy with Trump’s immigration policies in states like Texas.

A Cook Political Report survey of Texas Hispanic voters released last month found that nearly 66 percent of Hispanic voters in the state said they would be less likely to back a candidate who supported Trump’s immigration policies.

Trump, himself, acknowledged he struggled with messaging on the issue of immigration during a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump told a crowd of Hispanic and Latino supporters. “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.”

One Latino Democratic strategist emphasized the importance of tying Republicans to Trump’s messaging on the matter, even as they shift their rhetoric.

“I see a lot of people softening the way they’re talking about this stuff,” the Democratic strategist said. “He’s such a wild card, and I don’t know how much of what he says trickles down.”

“We need to show him his decisions, his actions, and that’s what matters,” the strategist added.

However, both Republicans and Democrats emphasize that immigration is not the top priority for Hispanic and Latino voters, noting that the economy remains top of mind for the voting bloc.

“If the economy were doing really well, we probably would not be having this conversation, certainly to the extent that we are,” Madrid said. “Immigration has become a compounding issue on top of the economy, but it is a secondary consideration.”

articles.body:
President Trump will rally voters in Nebraska Monday evening, as Republicans look to shore up support in a state where an unexpectedly competitive Senate race has put the GOP on defense.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) is facing independent Dan Osborn, who came within 7 points of Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) in 2024 and is now backed by state Democrats. Polling averages, including data from Decision Desk HQ , show a close contest in the deep-red state.

Trump’s visit is the latest stop in a swing through red states as the party faces a difficult midterm environment. Vice President Vance and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have also visited the Cornhusker State in recent months.

The event in Grand Island, Neb., is scheduled to begin at 7 p.m. EDT.

articles.body:
Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) said she supports all Democrats on the ballot in Texas, adding that this includes the Democratic Senate nominee who defeated her in the primary, James Talarico.

“I support all Democrats. Yes, that includes James Talarico, who I endorsed the day after the election, OK?” she said in a livestream on social media, the Texas Tribune reported Monday.

Crockett called Talarico to congratulate him on his win in the March 3 primary the following day, but no official statements or a formal endorsement have been released in the months since.

She lso not campaigned with Talarico, and Talarico’s name was not included in a list of 14 endorsements from Crockett’s FIRE PAC following its release last Monday, the Washington Post reported . The group has backed a wide swath of candidates across the country, including across Texas and in California and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Crockett blasted criticism over Talarico’s absence from the list, referring “lazy journalists” to her congratulatory post on the social platform X in March.

“Y’all are corny! I keep receipts. I’ll be happy when people either give a damn about FACTS or news media goes back to the news instead of deciding to ride the tabloid lane. NOW FOR THE 1000th time maybe write an article about KEN F*in PAXTON. Y’all all sound like corny groupie a– OPS!” she wrote on X last Tuesday, referring to GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

Crockett told CNN in August that she planned to focus on “ campaigning down ballot ” in Texas, making no mention of Talarico and his campaign. She pointed to all the energy spent on Democrat Beto O’Rourke’s campaign to defeat Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in 2018, only for O’Rourke to lose by a few points.

“And so for me, I think that making sure that people that maybe are getting overshadowed because it seems like it’s only about one big race, I think amplifying them, making sure that I can raise their profiles and introducing them to people, that’ll give something more to voters,” she told CNN’s Laura Coates at the time.

She has also said that she did not think it would help Talarico by sharing the stage with him at campaign events, instead choosing to campaign with Black candidates aiming to win in November.

“The best thing that I can do for James Talarico isn’t me standing on a stage with him,” Crockett told the San Antonio Observer in July, adding that help for those candidates could bring more Black Texans to the ballot box.

A Fox News poll released last Thursday showed Talarico leading Paxton 51-49. The race has become one of the most competitive in the nation as Democrats seek to reclaim control of the upper chamber.

President Trump chose to back Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) during the GOP primary runoff in May.

articles.body:
A new cloud of anxiety is hovering over the public amid reports of an infectious disease, a laboratory accident and a death.

The fact that the story comes out of Russia heightens American concerns rather than assuages them, raising dark talk of bioweapons, artificial intelligence and Kremlin secrecy.

“I hate to see them having it. It’s a rough disease,” he told reporters on Monday. “That’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army.”

He told another reporter: “We’re looking at it very strongly.”

The core concern here is pneumonic plague — not the infamous bubonic plague that ravaged the Middle Ages — and whether the Russian case, if officially confirmed, could spread. There are some reports that 200 people are already under medical observation in Siberia.

To Americans still traumatized by the peak years of the COVID-19 pandemic, the whole matter sounds an ominous warning bell.

But health experts who spoke to this column sought to calm incipient panic, noting that pneumonic plague — despite its horror-inducing name — is not particularly easily transmissible, usually requiring exposure in very close quarters.

In most instances, basic masking and isolation in hospital for those affected is “more than sufficient” to contain any broader dangers, said Dr. Mike Ryan, who led the World Health Organization’s emergence response division for eight years until 2025.

Ryan, like other experts who spoke to this column, also noted that it has yet to be officially confirmed that the Russian story even involves a death from plague.

Russian officials have acknowledged only that someone working at a lab in Siberia died from pneumonia of no clear origin. According to the New York Times, the authorities have also insisted that “no microorganisms linked to her professional activity were identified in the patient’s samples.”

But it’s easy to see why the matter has caused alarm.

The laboratory in question is the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia — a name that for some will carry echoes of the Wuhan Institute of Virology and the controversy over the origins of COVID.

In the Russian case, local reporting has indicated that the 28-year-old woman — named by CNN as Darya Shipilova — died after breaking a test tube.

Public skepticism has been further fueled by mixed messages from officials. According to the New York Times , the governor of a neighboring region posted a social media message about “the woman who died of plague” before amending that message by adding the word “possibly.”

A separate message from a town in the region about “a case of plague” was reportedly deleted.

“We don’t even know for sure that it’s plague,” professor Peter Hotez, the dean for the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine, told this column. “It certainly could be pneumonic plague, but we are not getting a lot of information out of the Russians.”

Hotez, like Ryan, also noted that even if plague is confirmed, that does not necessarily suggest malevolent weaponization.

“Even if it is pneumonic plague, it’s important not to jump to too many conclusions. This is right in the heart of where plague occurs naturally, so potentially she was working on a naturally occurring isolate.”

Larry Gostin, a Georgetown Law professor who specializes in public health, told this column that his “general view is that we don’t have to be, as Americans, particularly concerned” on the basis of what is known so far.

“Right now, we don’t have any evidence that they were designing a bioweapon, but it’s Russia, and we don’t know for sure,” Gostin said.

But he also noted that, separate from the specifics of events in Siberia, the story is landing at a time when concerns are growing about potential misuses of AI.

“I don’t want to be overly alarmist but this is one of the existential threats that we don’t talk about,” he said. “Normally, it’s a scenario of the AI agent taking over and doing harm to us. But a much more likely scenario is that a human with bad intentions will use the AI to be able to create a pandemic.”

All the experts who spoke to this column on Monday, including Gostin, stressed that they viewed the chances of a pandemic springing from his incident as low.

But they separately expressed broader concerns, including about pandemic preparedness in the United States.

“The likelihood that this is going to lead to a plague epidemic is probably pretty small,” said Hotez. “But it’s another reminder of the importance, on the U.S. side, that we don’t put pandemic preparedness on ice, because there are always these possibilities.”

On Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking of events in Russia, told reporters : “We’re watching and monitoring it closely. I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on. And we’re doing that.”

Ryan, the former WHO official, characterized Rubio’s position as “a reasonable stance.”

“Keeping a watching brief is perfectly sufficient at this point,” he said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.
